output.title: The hidden cost of demo theatre
output.body:
If you run a small business and have already tried ChatGPT, the quiet cost of demo theatre is easy to miss. You spend good time polishing a demo or testing one more tool, but the real workflow keeps waiting. The bill is not the demo itself. It is the work not done on something recurring.

For an owner-operator, that usually means repeated customer questions, manual invoice work, follow-ups, or lead handling. If the work is not repeating, AI is probably not the place to start. No shame in that; the machine can wait.

Bareni’s diagnostic stays bounded. We look for one recurring workflow, check honestly whether AI fits, and if it does, define a fixed-price pilot with clear measures. Timings and scope are intended, not guarantees. There is no mandatory roadmap gate in the middle, although a separate AI Strategy & Roadmap exists for customers who want strategy only.

Scope matters too. We currently decline high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work; bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests that depend on unsupported compliance or security claims. That is current scope discipline, not a claim that such work can never be automated.

A useful filter is simple: do you have one repeating workflow that reliably takes about 5–10 hours a week, has a measurable output, and keeps human approval on the risky part? If not, demo theatre is probably not the next thing to fix.
